templates.name: Principle plus case leads to consequence (S10 trade-off folded in)
Behaviour, design or content reveals a motive or belief (S12 example folded in)
Rule or timeline plus observation rejects a premise
X but not Y, so Z
Two cases or two accounts lead to a conditional or a common ground
Received view plus counterevidence leads to revision
Undercut leads to a hedged conclusion
Co-occurrence or repeated pattern leads to a link

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a poetic convention applied to a reader who ignores it
items.passage: Classical Tamil love poetry, composed roughly two thousand years ago, follows a convention in which each of five landscapes corresponds to a particular phase of love: mountains to the lovers’ union, forests to patient waiting, agricultural lands to quarreling, the seashore to anxious longing, and the wasteland to separation. Rather than explicitly naming a speaker’s emotions, poets could therefore let the vegetation, animals, and weather of the chosen setting evoke them. A contemporary reader who treats the flowering jasmine and gathering rain clouds of a forest poem as merely decorative scenery would thus be likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: take the poem to be a record of a particular forest that the poet knew well rather than an imagined setting.
mistake the poem for one about the lovers’ union, the phase of love that its rain and blossoms are meant to evoke.
fail to sense the long wait that the poem’s setting was meant to convey to its first audiences.
judge the poem to be less skillfully made than works in which poets state their speakers’ feelings directly.
items.explanation: The text says that in these poems each landscape signals a phase of love, with forests signaling patient waiting, and that poets let a setting’s details imply emotions instead of naming them. A reader who sees the forest poem’s jasmine and rain clouds only as scenery would therefore not notice the waiting that the setting was meant to convey, a meaning the poem’s original audiences would have grasped.

A.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether the settings were real places the poets knew; its point is what the settings signal about the speaker’s emotions.

B.why_wrong: The convention pairs union with mountains, not forests; a forest poem’s imagery signals patient waiting, so the imagery is not meant to evoke union.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how readers would rate the poem’s quality; it explains only what such a reader would fail to notice.

sources.what: Sangam landscapes: mountains with union, forests with waiting, cropland with quarreling, seashore with pining, desert with separation; the imagery conveys the mood

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature). S2: a convention (landscape signals phase of love, emotion left implicit) applied to a reader who ignores it; two steps (forest = waiting; scenery-only reading misses it). Distractors: OUT (real place), MIX (union belongs to mountains), REC (quality). Jasmine is the forest (mullai) flower.

fixes: key C paraphrased off the passage’s “patient waiting” (now “fail to sense the long wait that the poem’s setting was meant to convey to its first audiences”), so the key no longer echoes the passage and B (right code, wrong phase) carries the weight; re-solved blind, C only
review.source_checked: Wikipedia Sangam landscape: forest (mullai) = waiting, mountains = union, jasmine is the mullai flower, imagery conveys the mood

band7.why: Two steps (forest means waiting; a scenery-only reading loses that coded emotion). After the fix the key no longer echoes the passage, and B is a near miss that applies the code but swaps the phase (union belongs to mountains); A and D stay plain OUT and REC. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a viewing practice applied to the painter who plans for it
items.passage: Chinese handscrolls, some of which extend more than ten meters, were not intended to be displayed on a wall and comprehended at a glance. Instead, a viewer seated at a table unrolled the painting from right to left, examining a section approximately the width of his or her shoulders and then rerolling it before exposing the next, so that only a portion of the composition was ever visible at once. An artist designing an extended landscape in this format could therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: arrange its scenes so that a viewer would come upon them one after another, in an order the artist had chosen.
leave it to each viewer, rather than to the arrangement of the scenes, to decide where a journey through the landscape would begin.
make each section of the landscape exactly as wide as the shoulders of a typical viewer.
include a wider range of scenery than painters of scrolls meant to hang on a wall usually did.
items.explanation: Because a handscroll was unrolled from right to left and seen only one section at a time, every viewer met its parts in the same sequence. An artist could therefore plan the order in which a viewer would come upon each scene, unfolding the landscape over time rather than presenting it all at once.

B.why_wrong: Viewers always unrolled the scroll from right to left, so the starting point and the sequence of scenes were set by the painting itself, not chosen by each viewer.

C.why_wrong: The text uses shoulder width only to describe how much of the scroll a viewer saw at once; nothing suggests painters divided the landscape into sections of that exact size.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares the variety of scenery in handscrolls with that in hanging scrolls.

sources.what: handscrolls were unrolled from right to left, a shoulder-width section at a time, each section rerolled before the next

items.notes: Area: humanities (art history). S2: a viewing practice (sequential, partial view) applied to the painter's planning; two steps (only part visible, fixed direction, so the painter controls the order). Distractors: REV (viewer chooses the start), ECHO (shoulder width), CMP (hanging scrolls). Length 'more than ten meters' per the Met's 39-foot Eighteen Songs scroll.

review.source_checked: Met handscroll essay (direct fetch blocked by a bot check; its text confirmed through search results): unrolled right to left, a shoulder-width section at a time, each rerolled before the next

band7.why: Two steps (only a shoulder-width section visible, unrolled in a fixed direction, so the painter sets the order of scenes); key paraphrased. D (wider scenery than hanging scrolls) is a tempting unsupported comparison; B (reversal) and C (shoulder-width echo) each fall to one stated fact. Band 6 near its easy edge.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: what an improvised form leaves out of its written records
items.passage: Commedia dell’arte troupes, which performed in Italy and France from the mid-1500s onward, worked from scenarios: brief outlines, often posted backstage, that listed each scene’s entrances, exits, and main events. Within that frame the actors improvised their dialogue and worked in lazzi, rehearsed comic routines that could be fitted into almost any plot, and audiences came chiefly to see favorite performers rather than to follow the stories. Historians who rely on the fifty scenarios that actor Flaminio Scala published in 1611 to explain the form’s popularity therefore face the difficulty that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the scenarios describe the troupes’ comic routines in far greater detail than they describe the events of each plot.
the scenarios record the actors’ dialogue in full but leave out the comic routines that were fitted into each plot.
Scala likely left out of his collection the scenes that audiences of his day enjoyed most.
what most drew audiences to the performances is largely absent from the outlines that survive.
items.explanation: A scenario recorded only the outline of a performance: entrances, exits, and main events. The dialogue and comic routines were supplied by the actors, and audiences came mainly for those performers, not for the stories. So the written scenarios preserve the part audiences cared least about and leave out much of what made the form popular.

A.why_wrong: The scenarios listed entrances, exits, and events; the comic routines and dialogue were left to the actors, so the outlines record plots more fully than routines, not the reverse.

B.why_wrong: The comic routines are indeed missing from the outlines, but the actors improvised their dialogue, so the scenarios could not have recorded it; they list only entrances, exits, and main events.

C.why_wrong: What the scenarios lack is the improvised dialogue and routines, not whole scenes; the outlines list every scene’s events, and nothing suggests Scala omitted scenes.

sources.what: commedia performances were largely improvised on scenarios that gave some semblance of plot; audiences came to see the performers, plotlines secondary; Scala's scenarios published in the early 17th century

items.notes: Area: humanities (theater history). S2: improvised form plus audience preference applied to historians who use the written outlines; two steps (outlines record plot only; audiences came for what was improvised). Distractors: REV (routines recorded in detail), CMP (France vs Italy), MIX (scenes vs dialogue). Scala's Il teatro delle favole rappresentative, 1611, fifty scenarios.

fixes: B (France vs Italy, a plain unsupported comparison) rebuilt as a half-right claim: the outlines do leave out the routines but cannot record the improvised dialogue; re-solved blind, D only
review.source_checked: Wikipedia commedia dell’arte: improvised on scenarios, audiences came to see the performers, plot secondary; Scala 1611, 50 scenarios

band7.why: Two steps (the outlines record only plot; audiences came for the improvised performers); key paraphrased (“what most drew audiences”). A, B and C are all near misses about what the written record holds, B now half right. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a notational practice applied to modern performances of one composer
items.passage: In seventeenth-century Italy, composers of solo vocal music typically notated only the singer’s melody and a bass line; during performance, a keyboard or lute player improvised chords above that bass, guided, when composers supplied them, by small numerals specifying the intended harmonies. The Venetian composer Barbara Strozzi, who published several collections of arias in the mid-1600s, generally left her bass lines without such numerals, and some of her harmonic progressions are so unconventional that present-day accompanists struggle to devise suitable chords. Two modern performances that each reproduce her printed notes exactly could thus ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: differ in their vocal melodies, since singers of Strozzi’s time were expected to invent their own lines above the bass.
differ noticeably in the harmonies heard beneath the singer’s voice, even though neither accompanist departs from anything Strozzi wrote.
sound more alike than performances of arias that include numerals, since players would have fewer choices to make.
reveal which chords Strozzi intended, provided that both players had studied the other arias in her collections.
items.explanation: Strozzi’s printed arias give the melody and the bass line but no numerals, so the chords above the bass are left to each player, and her unusual progressions make the right chords hard to determine. Two players who both play exactly what she printed could therefore choose different harmonies, making the performances sound different without either one departing from the score.

A.why_wrong: The text says composers wrote out the singer’s melody; what performers supplied was the chords above the bass, so the melodies would not differ.

C.why_wrong: Without numerals, players have more choices to make, not fewer, so performances would be less alike than performances guided by numerals.

D.why_wrong: The text says present-day players struggle to find fitting chords and gives no basis for thinking that studying her other arias would reveal the chords she intended.

sources.what: Strozzi's arias for solo voice and basso continuo are unfigured, and some progressions are so unusual that continuo players struggle to provide a sensible realization (de Goede, Leeds 2008)

items.notes: Area: humanities (music). S2: continuo practice (bass written, chords improvised, numerals optional) plus Strozzi's unfigured basses applied to two faithful modern performances; two steps. Distractors: MIX (melody), REV (more alike), EXT (other arias reveal intent).

review.source_checked: de Goede, Leeds 2008 abstract: Strozzi’s arias are unfigured and some progressions are so outlandish that a sensible continuo realization seems almost impossible

band7.why: Two steps (no numerals, so the chords are each player’s choice; the unusual progressions widen that choice) to a consequence for two faithful performances. A (melodies differ) and D (her other arias reveal intent) are partly right; C a reversal. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a land-division principle applied to residents who clear upland forest
items.passage: Before Western contact, Native Hawaiians divided each island into ahupuaʻa, land divisions that typically extended from the forested uplands to the offshore reef. A single community could thereby harvest timber and bird feathers in the mountains, cultivate taro on the lower slopes, and fish along the coastline. Because rainfall on the uplands drained through each division in streams that transported soil and debris toward the sea, residents who cleared excessive amounts of their upland forest would likely have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: damaged the farmland and fishing grounds on which their own community relied farther downslope.
lost a source of timber and feathers, although the effects of the clearing would have stayed in the uplands.
harmed chiefly neighboring communities, whose lands lay downstream of the cleared forest.
gained timber that they could exchange for fish caught in other communities’ waters.
items.explanation: Each ahupuaʻa ran from the uplands to the reef, so a community’s forest, farmland, and fishing grounds lay within the same unit, and the unit’s streams carried soil and debris from the uplands down toward the sea. Clearing the upland forest would therefore have sent material down onto the community’s own taro fields and shoreline, harming resources it depended on.

B.why_wrong: Clearing the forest would remove timber and feathers, but the text says streams carried soil and debris down through the unit, so the effects would not have stayed in the uplands.

C.why_wrong: Each unit ran from the uplands down to the reef, so the land downstream of a community’s forest was its own farmland and shore, not a neighbor’s.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about trade between communities; it stresses that each unit supplied its community with resources from mountain to sea.

sources.what: ahupuaʻa: wedge-shaped land divisions running from the uplands to the sea, giving each community forest, farmland and ocean resources

items.notes: Area: history and anthropology (Native Hawaiian land use). S2: the mountain-to-sea unit plus downhill drainage applied to upland clearing; two steps (same community owns both ends; streams carry the damage down). Distractors: PART (timber loss only), MIX (neighbors downstream), OUT (trade). The cited claim is the mountain-to-sea unit; the downhill drainage premise is general knowledge stated in the passage, not part of the cited claim. Written with the Hawaiian spelling and okina.

review.source_checked: NPS ahupuaʻa page: mountain to sea, forest for timber and bird collection, taro farming, fish; the downhill-runoff premise is general knowledge stated in the passage

band7.why: Two steps (one unit runs from mountain to reef; streams carry soil downhill) to harm to the same community. B keeps the timber loss and C keeps the downstream harm with the wrong owner; D off-topic trade. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 prediction: a dispersal cost applied to selection in fragmented city habitat
items.passage: The weed Crepis sancta produces two types of seeds: lightweight ones with feathery tufts that enable wind dispersal, and heavier ones that simply fall beside the parent plant. In Montpellier, France, the species also inhabits the small squares of soil surrounding street trees, each one isolated within an expanse of pavement. Reasoning that a wind-dispersed seed released from such a patch would seldom land anywhere suitable for germination, ecologist Pierre-Olivier Cheptou and colleagues predicted that in these urban populations, natural selection would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: reduce the total number of seeds that each plant produces, since so many of the seeds would be wasted on pavement.
favor plants growing in the largest patches of soil over those in the smallest, whatever kinds of seeds they produce.
favor plants that put a larger share of their seeds into the kind that falls close to the parent.
make both kinds of seeds heavier in city plants than in plants of the species growing in the surrounding countryside.
items.explanation: A wind-borne seed released from a small patch surrounded by pavement will rarely reach soil, while a seed that drops beside its parent lands in the patch. Plants that produce more of the dropping seeds should therefore leave more offspring, so the researchers expected selection to shift city plants toward that kind of seed.

A.why_wrong: The problem the text describes is which kind of seed is produced, since the heavy seeds still land in soil; nothing suggests that producing fewer seeds overall would help.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares patches of different sizes; the researchers’ reasoning concerns which kind of seed reaches soil, not patch size.

D.why_wrong: Selection would favor the seeds that drop near the parent over the wind-borne ones; the text gives no reason for wind-borne seeds to become heavier too, and it never compares city plants with rural ones.

sources.what: Crepis sancta in Montpellier tree-base patches: dispersing seeds rarely settle in a patch, and urban populations evolved a higher proportion of nondispersing seeds (Cheptou et al. 2008, PNAS)

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolutionary ecology). S2: dispersal cost in fragmented habitat applied as a prediction about selection (the 3.2 'anticipated that' shape); two steps (wind seeds mostly lost; plants making more dropping seeds leave more offspring). Distractors: MIX (total number), VAR (patch size), MIX/CMP (both kinds heavier, city vs countryside).

review.source_checked: Cheptou et al. 2008 PNAS (PMC): dispersing seeds fall on concrete, urban patches have a higher share of nondispersing seeds; the introduction states the expectation that urban selection should reduce dispersal

band7.why: Two steps (wind seeds land on pavement; plants that make more dropping seeds leave more offspring) to a prediction about selection. A and D are partly right (seeds wasted; heavier seeds); B a wrong variable. Band 6.

items.subtype: T2 belief: an added procedure reveals what officials thought could still go wrong (counterfactual lead-in)
items.passage: Under China’s Song dynasty (960–1279), the civil service examinations became the main route into government office for ambitious young men, and success could change the fortunes of a candidate’s whole family. To keep examiners from favoring candidates with powerful connections, officials adopted two procedures. First, each candidate’s name was covered on the answer papers. Second, clerks copied out every answer by hand, and examiners graded only these copies, never the original papers that the candidates themselves had written. The second procedure suggests that officials believed that if the answers had not been copied, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: examiners would have struggled to read answers written in haste, which would have delayed the grading of thousands of papers.
an examiner acquainted with a candidate might still have identified that candidate’s paper despite the covered name.
clerks would have been able to alter the wording of answers to benefit candidates they personally knew.
candidates seated near one another could have copied each other’s answers without being detected.
items.explanation: Both procedures were meant to keep examiners from favoring well-connected candidates, and names were already hidden by the first one. Having clerks copy every answer adds protection only if something besides the name could reveal who wrote a paper, such as the candidate’s handwriting. So officials must have thought that, without copying, an examiner who knew a candidate could still recognize that candidate’s paper.

A.why_wrong: The text presents both procedures as safeguards against favoritism, not as ways to make answers easier to read or to speed up grading.

C.why_wrong: It is the copying that puts answers in clerks’ hands; without it, clerks would not handle the answers at all, so the risk of clerks altering them would not arise.

D.why_wrong: The text concerns how examiners graded papers, not whether candidates could copy from one another while taking the examination.

sources.what: Teng Lu: from the early Northern Song, each examination answer was copied onto another paper so that examiners could not recognize candidates' handwriting

items.notes: Area: history (Chinese civil service examinations). S9: a design choice reveals officials' belief; two steps (names already hidden, so copying must target another identifier: handwriting). Counterfactual lead-in as in 3.7, worded differently. Distractors: CAUSE (legibility), REV (clerks altering), OUT (candidates cheating).

review.source_checked: Peking University Library page: Teng Lu, answers copied onto another paper so examiners could not recognize a candidate’s handwriting

band7.why: A belief inferred from a design choice under a counterfactual lead-in: names were already hidden, so copying must guard against handwriting. A (legibility) is a real rival motive, C reverses who handles the answers, D plays on “copied”. Band 6, near the band-7 T2 profile but with the clue one sentence away.

items.subtype: T1 dating: a land-bridge timeline plus an absence rejects early arrival
items.passage: People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and for tens of thousands of years afterward Tasmania remained connected to the mainland by a land bridge, permitting animals and people to travel between the two until rising seas submerged it approximately 12,000 years ago. Dingoes, which could have reached Australia only aboard human vessels, were widespread across the entire mainland when European colonists arrived, and their skeletal remains there have been radiocarbon dated to more than 3,000 years ago. Yet dingoes are entirely absent from Tasmania’s fossil record, a distribution suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: dingoes reached Australia after people did but before the land bridge to Tasmania was submerged.
the first people to reach Tasmania brought dogs of a different kind, which prevented dingoes from establishing themselves there.
dingoes could not have reached the mainland any earlier than about 3,000 years ago.
dingoes arrived in Australia long after its first human inhabitants rather than accompanying them.
items.explanation: Until about 12,000 years ago, animals could walk from the mainland to Tasmania, so if dingoes had been on the mainland then, they would likely have reached Tasmania too. Their absence from Tasmania’s fossil record suggests that they arrived only after the land bridge was submerged, which was tens of thousands of years after people first reached Australia.

A.why_wrong: Dingoes did arrive after people, but if they had come while the land bridge still stood, they could have walked to Tasmania as other animals did; their absence from Tasmania’s fossil record points to arrival after the bridge was submerged.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions any other dogs in Tasmania or anything that kept dingoes out other than the timing of the land bridge’s submergence.

C.why_wrong: Dingo remains on the mainland are dated to more than 3,000 years ago, which shows that dingoes were there earlier than that, not that they could not have arrived earlier.

sources.what: dingoes are not found in the fossil record of Tasmania and apparently arrived after Tasmania separated from the mainland due to rising sea levels; oldest Madura Cave dingo bones directly dated to 3,348 to 3,081 years ago

items.notes: Area: natural science and archaeology (biogeography). S3: land-bridge timeline plus absence rejects arrival with the first settlers; two steps (absence implies arrival after about 12,000 years ago; that is long after people arrived). Distractors: REV (lived there, died out), OUT (other dogs), REV of the date bound (3,000 years as a ceiling instead of a floor). Human arrival of at least 50,000 years is general knowledge, not part of the cited claim.

fixes: A (disappeared from Tasmania, killed by the stated absence) rebuilt to keep the key’s true half (after people) and break on timing (before the bridge was submerged); re-solved blind, D only
review.source_checked: Wikipedia Dingo: absent from Tasmania’s fossil record, arrived after Tasmania was cut off by rising seas, Madura Cave bones dated 3,348 to 3,081 years ago, came by boat

band7.why: Two steps (the bridge let animals cross until about 12,000 years ago, so absence means later arrival; that is long after the first people). A now keeps the key’s “after people” and breaks on timing; C turns the 3,000-year floor into a ceiling; B off-topic. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: internal injury in most bats but contact injury in only half
items.passage: Bats are killed in considerable numbers at wind farms, and the most straightforward explanation is that they collide with the rotating turbine blades. When biologist Erin Baerwald and colleagues performed necropsies on bats collected beneath turbines in Alberta, Canada, however, they found that about 90 percent exhibited internal hemorrhaging consistent with barotrauma, lung damage caused by the abrupt drop in air pressure near moving blades, whereas only approximately half showed evidence of direct contact. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: measures designed only to keep bats from striking the turbines’ blades would likely leave a large share of these deaths unprevented.
most of the bats with internal hemorrhaging were probably injured when they fell to the ground after being struck.
barotrauma, rather than collision with the blades, accounts for all of the bat deaths at wind farms.
a turbine’s drop in air pressure injures bats only after they have already collided with one of its blades.
items.explanation: About 90 percent of the bats had internal injuries from the pressure drop near the blades, but only about half had been struck. Many bats were therefore killed without touching a blade, so steps that only prevent collisions would not stop those deaths.

B.why_wrong: Only about half of the bats showed signs of being struck, while about 90 percent had internal bleeding, so many of the bats with internal bleeding had not been struck at all.

C.why_wrong: About half of the bats showed signs of direct contact with the blades, so collisions likely caused some of the deaths; the findings show that barotrauma is common, not that it is the only cause.

D.why_wrong: Internal injuries appeared in far more bats than signs of contact did, so the pressure drop must have harmed many bats that never collided with a blade.

sources.what: 90% of bat fatalities at an Alberta wind farm involved internal haemorrhaging consistent with barotrauma; direct contact with blades accounted for only about half (Baerwald et al. 2008, Current Biology)

items.notes: Area: natural science (wildlife ecology). S6: internal injury in about 90 percent but contact in about half, so many died without contact; key applies that to collision-only measures (two steps). Distractors: CAUSE (fall injuries), CMP (birds, attraction), MIX (pressure only after collision). Key is the longest option here by design (batch key-longest rate).

fixes: C (bats vs birds, a plain off-topic comparison) rebuilt as an overreach from the 90 percent figure (barotrauma accounts for all deaths), which the “about half” contact figure refutes; re-solved blind, A only
review.source_checked: ScienceDaily 2008: Baerwald (University of Calgary), 90 percent internal hemorrhaging, about half with evidence of blade contact

band7.why: A numbers step (about 90 against about 50 percent, so many bats died without contact) then a consequence for collision-only measures. B a rival mechanism, C now an overreach from the 90 percent, D reverses the order of injuries. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion from opposite rankings on practice and test
items.passage: In a study by psychologists Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor, undergraduates learned to calculate the volumes of four unfamiliar geometric solids and then completed a set of practice problems in two sessions held a week apart. For some students the problems were blocked, with all the problems for one solid preceding those for the next; for others, identical problems were randomly intermixed. During practice, the blocked group correctly answered 89% of the problems and the intermixed group only 60%, yet on a test administered a week after the final session, the intermixed group scored 63% and the blocked group only 20%, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: students who perform poorly during practice tend to study more on their own before they are tested.
the blocked group’s low test scores most likely resulted from that group’s having worked fewer practice problems.
how accurately students solve problems during practice may be a misleading indication of how much they will retain.
intermixed practice improves later test performance only when the practice sessions are held a week or more apart.
items.explanation: The group that did better during practice, the blocked group, did far worse on the test a week later, while the group that struggled during practice did far better. Success during practice therefore did not predict how much students remembered, so practice performance may be a poor guide to later learning.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no information about any studying students did outside the two practice sessions.

B.why_wrong: The text says the two groups worked identical problems, only in a different order, so the blocked group did not work fewer problems.

D.why_wrong: Both groups practiced on the same schedule, with sessions a week apart, so the study gives no basis for saying that the benefit of intermixing depends on that spacing.

sources.what: Rohrer and Taylor 2007, Experiment 2: blocked practice 89% vs mixed 60% correct during practice; test a week later mixed 63% vs blocked 20%

items.notes: Area: social science (educational psychology). S1 hard: the comparison hides in two pairs of numbers that rank the groups in opposite orders (the 3.21 pattern); two steps (practice favors blocked, test favors intermixed; so practice scores mislead). Figures checked against the paper's text (Instructional Science 35, 2007). Distractors: CAUSE, REV (fewer problems), FUT.

fixes: D (an odd counterfactual about session spacing and practice scores) rebuilt as an overreach (intermixing helps only with a week or more between sessions); re-solved blind, C only
review.source_checked: USF Digital Commons abstract: Rohrer and Taylor 2007, Experiment 2 blocked vs mixed practice, test one week later vastly better after mixed practice (exact percentages are the writer’s check of the paper, smaller detail)

band7.why: Opposite rankings on practice and test lead to a general conclusion about practice scores; key paraphrased. A a rival cause, B falls to “identical problems”, D now an overreach on spacing. Band 6.

items.subtype: T2 common ground: two rival accounts share an implication
items.passage: Medieval pilgrims to the shrine of Thomas Becket in Canterbury frequently purchased inexpensive badges of lead and tin there, which they attached to their hats or clothing as souvenirs of the journey. Hundreds of these badges have since been recovered from the riverbank mud of the Thames in London. Some historians propose that returning pilgrims deliberately threw their badges into the river, perhaps as a symbolic expression of gratitude for a safe return; others maintain that the badges were simply discarded with household refuse once they had broken or outlived their usefulness. Whichever interpretation is correct, both groups would likely agree that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: pilgrims attached little value to their badges once they had returned home.
many pilgrims carried their badges away from Canterbury rather than leaving them at the shrine.
the badges recovered from the Thames were most likely manufactured in London rather than in Canterbury.
throwing badges into rivers was a custom that pilgrims learned during their visits to Canterbury.
items.explanation: Both explanations describe badges ending up in the Thames in London, either thrown in by returning pilgrims or dumped with household rubbish there. Either way, the badges bought at Canterbury must first have traveled home with their owners. So both groups of historians would agree that many pilgrims took their badges away from the shrine.

A.why_wrong: This fits only the view that badges were thrown out as rubbish; historians who think pilgrims offered their badges as a gesture of thanks would not agree that pilgrims valued them little.

C.why_wrong: The text says pilgrims bought the badges at the Canterbury shrine, and neither account suggests they were made in London.

D.why_wrong: This fits only the view that badges were deliberately thrown into the river, and even that view does not say where such a custom began.

sources.what: many pilgrim badges recovered from the Thames; debated whether thrown into the water deliberately as a symbolic gesture or dumped as household waste after they had broken or outlived their use

items.notes: Area: history (medieval pilgrimage). S7: two accounts and their common ground (the 3.15 shape, new wording); two steps (both accounts place the badges in London; so they were carried from Canterbury). Distractors: PART (rubbish view only), REV (made in London), PART (offering view only).

review.source_checked: The Becket Story (Canterbury Christ Church): many badges recovered from the Thames; debate whether thrown in as a symbolic gesture or discarded as household rubbish once broken or outlived their use

band7.why: Common ground of two accounts: both put Canterbury badges in the London Thames, so pilgrims carried them away. A and D each fit only one account (partly right); C a reversal. Band 6.

items.subtype: T5 negative frame: evidence casts doubt on a received view
items.passage: Wine buyers often treat a medal from a panel of expert judges as a dependable indicator of quality. Winemaker Robert Hodgson examined this belief at the California State Fair wine competition by having judges unknowingly evaluate three samples poured from the same bottle. Only about 10 percent consistently scored all three within a single medal category, and some considered the identical wine deserving of bronze once and gold another time, results that call into question the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: expert judges distinguish between wines made from different grape varieties more reliably than between wines made from the same variety.
the judges evaluated the wines they rated highly more consistently than the wines they rated poorly.
a wine’s result at such a competition may depend partly on chance rather than solely on the wine itself.
a medal won at such a competition reflects an assessment of the wine that would likely be repeated if the wine were judged again.
items.explanation: Judges given the same wine three times rarely scored it consistently, and some gave it bronze one time and gold another. A medal is therefore not a judgment that would reliably be repeated, which undermines the assumption that a medal tells buyers something stable about a wine’s quality.

A.why_wrong: The study tested the same wine poured three times; it never compared wines made from different grape varieties.

B.why_wrong: The text reports how inconsistent the judges were overall but never compares their consistency on wines they liked with their consistency on wines they disliked.

C.why_wrong: The results support this idea rather than casting doubt on it: if the same wine can earn bronze or gold, chance plays a part in a wine’s result.

sources.what: California State Fair judges given triplicate samples from the same bottle: about 10 percent replicated their score within a single medal group; another 10 percent on occasion scored the same wine Bronze to Gold (Hodgson 2008, Journal of Wine Economics)

items.notes: Area: social science (consumer behavior, wine economics). S11 with the negative frame (the 2.4 shape); key states the view undercut, POL trap states what the evidence supports. Two steps (judges inconsistent on identical wine; so a medal is not a repeatable judgment). Distractors: VAR, CMP, POL. Hodgson was also a judge at the event; not mentioned.

review.source_checked: Hodgson 2008, Journal of Wine Economics abstract: triplicate samples from the same bottle, about 10 percent replicated within one medal group, another 10 percent scored the same wine bronze to gold

band7.why: Negative frame: the key states the view the evidence undercuts and C is the polarity trap stating what the evidence supports. A and B stay plain “never compared” options (a sharper B risked a second defensible answer). Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 revision: evidence revises a received view
items.passage: The forests of Amazonia have often been portrayed as largely untouched by humans before the arrival of Europeans. Ecologist Carolina Levis and colleagues tested this view by comparing tree surveys from across the basin with the locations of more than 3,000 archaeological sites. They found that 85 tree species domesticated by Indigenous peoples, including the Brazil nut and cacao, were five times more likely than other species to rank among the forest’s most abundant trees. These domesticated species were also especially common near archaeological sites, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: people who lived in Amazonia long ago may have helped shape the composition of the forests that grow there today.
Indigenous peoples in Amazonia domesticated a larger number of tree species than peoples in any other part of the world did.
domesticated tree species grow more quickly than wild species do in the nutrient-poor soils of Amazonia.
most of the forest’s abundant tree species were domesticated before the arrival of Europeans.
items.explanation: Species that Indigenous peoples domesticated are unusually common in Amazonian forests, and they are especially common near places where people lived long ago. This pattern suggests that past human activity helped determine which trees fill the forests today, so the forests were not untouched before Europeans arrived.

B.why_wrong: The study looked only at Amazonia; the text gives no information about how many tree species were domesticated anywhere else.

C.why_wrong: The text never discusses growth rates or soils; it links the domesticated species’ abundance to past human activity, shown by their concentration near archaeological sites.

D.why_wrong: The text says domesticated species were more likely than others to be among the most abundant trees, not that most abundant species were domesticated.

sources.what: 85 domesticated woody species five times more likely than non-domesticated species to be hyperdominant, and more abundant near archaeological sites (Levis et al. 2017, Science)

items.notes: Area: natural science and archaeology (historical ecology). S11: received view (untouched forest) revised by evidence; key one level more general than the data. Distractors: CMP, CAUSE, EXT (most abundant species domesticated).

review.source_checked: ScienceDaily 2017: Levis et al., 85 domesticated species five times more likely to be common, more than 3,000 archaeological sites, more common near sites

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a composition rule applied to a long poem
items.passage: Renga, a form of Japanese linked verse that flourished from the fourteenth to the sixteenth centuries, was typically composed collaboratively by several poets who took turns contributing stanzas at a single gathering. Each new stanza had to connect with the stanza immediately preceding it, whether through a shared image, a contrast, or a shift of perspective. However, a stanza was not permitted to connect with the stanza that had come before that one. Consequently, a long renga would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: be easier for readers to follow from start to finish than a poem of similar length written by a single author.
return at regular intervals to the image with which its opening stanza began.
move from one subject to another rather than developing a single story from beginning to end.
contain fewer images drawn from nature than shorter forms of Japanese poetry did.
items.explanation: Each stanza could link only to the one just before it and not to the one before that, so no image or story could be carried forward across several stanzas. A long renga would therefore keep shifting from subject to subject instead of developing one story throughout.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares how easy renga and poems by a single author are to follow.

B.why_wrong: Because a stanza could not link back even two stanzas, returning regularly to the opening image would go against the rule the text describes.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how often renga used images from nature or about other forms of Japanese poetry.

sources.what: each verse in renga must relate to the verse immediately preceding it but may not relate to the verse two positions earlier; no logical or narrative continuity over more than two verses

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature). S2: a linking rule applied to a whole poem. Distractors: CMP (single author), REV (returns to the opening image), CMP (nature imagery).

review.source_checked: PAJLS (Brandeis) article: each renga verse must relate to the verse immediately before it but may not relate to the verse two before; no narrative continuity beyond two verses

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a price rule applied to a household in a bad harvest year
items.passage: Under England’s Assize of Bread and Ale, a statute dating to the 1260s, bakers sold standard loaves at fixed prices, such as a farthing, which was one quarter of a penny. What fluctuated instead was the weight: local authorities consulted a schedule specifying how heavy a farthing loaf had to be at each prevailing price of wheat, and the required weight decreased as wheat became more expensive. Consequently, in a year when disastrous harvests drove up the price of wheat, a household spending its customary farthing on bread would have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: paid more than a farthing for a loaf weighing the same amount as in other years.
received a smaller loaf than it would have received in a year of plentiful harvests.
been permitted to buy bread only from bakers whom local officials had approved.
received a loaf of the customary weight that the baker had made from a grain less costly than wheat.
items.explanation: The price of a loaf stayed fixed, but the weight a farthing bought fell when wheat grew more expensive. Poor harvests raise the price of wheat, so in such a year a family paying its usual farthing would get a lighter, smaller loaf.

A.why_wrong: The text says loaves were sold at fixed prices and only their weight changed, so the family would not pay more than a farthing.

C.why_wrong: The text says officials set loaf weights; it says nothing about officials approving which bakers people could buy from.

D.why_wrong: The text describes adjusting the loaf’s weight, not changing its grain, and gives no basis for thinking bakers switched to cheaper grains.

sources.what: the Assize of Bread and Ale (c. 1266) regulated the price, weight and quality of bread; bread prices were fixed while the weight of a loaf varied with the price of grain

items.notes: Area: history (medieval economic regulation). S2 medium: fixed price, variable weight applied to a bad harvest year. Distractors: REV (price rises), OUT (approved bakers), CAUSE (cheaper grain).

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Assize of Bread and Ale: bread price always the same, weight of a farthing loaf fell with every rise in the price of wheat

items.subtype: T1 conclusion from a two-sign comparison
items.passage: Health care professionals often clean their hands less frequently than hospital guidelines recommend, a lapse that can allow infections to spread from one patient to another. To determine whether the wording of reminders matters, management researchers Adam Grant and David Hofmann posted signs above the soap and sanitizing-gel dispensers in a US hospital. Some signs read “Hand hygiene prevents you from catching diseases,” while others read “Hand hygiene prevents patients from catching diseases.” Over the following two weeks, use of soap and gel rose by about a third at dispensers displaying the patient-focused sign but remained essentially unchanged at those displaying the sign about professionals’ own health, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: signs posted directly above dispensers change behavior more effectively than reminders delivered during staff training sessions.
health care workers seldom read the signs that hospitals post near soap and gel dispensers.
signs that mention diseases encourage hand washing more than signs that simply explain how to use a dispenser do.
reminding health care workers of the risks their behavior poses to others may motivate them more than reminding them of risks to themselves.
items.explanation: The two signs differed only in whose health the hand washing protected. Use of soap and gel rose noticeably only where the sign mentioned patients, so a reminder about protecting others appears to motivate health care workers more than a reminder about protecting themselves.

A.why_wrong: The study compared the wording of two signs; it never compared signs with training sessions.

B.why_wrong: Changing one word on a sign changed how much soap and gel workers used, which indicates that workers did notice the signs.

C.why_wrong: The text describes no signs that only explain how to use a dispenser, and the sign about workers’ own risk of disease produced no change, so mentioning diseases alone did not encourage hand washing.

sources.what: signs reading 'Hand hygiene prevents patients from catching diseases' raised soap and gel use; signs about catching diseases oneself did not (Grant and Hofmann 2011, Psychological Science)

items.notes: Area: social science (organizational psychology). S1: groups differ in one factor (whose health the sign names). Distractors: VAR (training), REV (signs unread), CMP (disease signs vs instruction signs; the study's control sign is left out of the passage because the cited release does not describe it). Key is the longest option here by design.

fixes: why_wrong A said the study compared “three signs”; the passage describes two (fixed), and the subtype’s “three-way” likewise
review.source_checked: APS release: Grant and Hofmann, the two sign wordings, patient sign raised use by 33 percent over two weeks, the self-focused sign had no measurable effect

items.subtype: T5 hedge: a rival explanation undercuts the usual account
items.passage: Many songbirds engage in “anting,” rubbing ants through their feathers. Because the ants involved typically belong to species that spray formic acid, the behavior has often been interpreted as a method of ridding plumage of mites and other parasites. However, biologists Thomas Eisner and Daniel Aneshansley observed that blue jays usually swallowed the ants they had rubbed through their feathers, and that jays offered ants whose acid sacs had been surgically removed generally ate them without anting. It therefore seems that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the usual explanation of anting as a defense against feather parasites may be incomplete.
formic acid is less effective at killing feather mites than biologists had long believed.
blue jays seldom carry feather parasites and so have little need to use ants against them.
anting cannot help birds keep their feathers free of parasites.
items.explanation: The jays usually ate the ants after anting, and they skipped anting when an ant’s acid sac had already been removed. That pattern fits a different purpose, getting rid of the acid so the ant can be eaten, so the familiar parasite explanation may not tell the whole story.

B.why_wrong: The text reports nothing about how well formic acid kills mites; the observations concern when the jays anted and what they did with the ants.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how many parasites blue jays carry.

D.why_wrong: The observations suggest anting has another purpose, but they do not show that it is useless against parasites.

sources.what: blue jays ate the ants they subjected to anting; ants with the acid sac excised were generally eaten without anting; anting renders ants fit for ingestion (Eisner and Aneshansley 2008, Chemoecology)

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S5: usual account undercut by a rival (food preparation), so the account is not established; lead-in and option frames differ from 2.18. Distractors: OUT, OUT, EXT.

review.source_checked: Eisner and Aneshansley 2008, Chemoecology (PMC): ants swallowed after anting, ants with acid sacs removed eaten without anting, anting renders ants fit for ingestion

items.subtype: T1 conditional: opposite outcomes in two selling formats lead to a depends-on conclusion
items.passage: Marketing researchers Rajesh Bagchi and Amar Cheema have argued that the color red heightens physiological arousal and, consequently, aggressiveness. In an analysis of eBay auctions and in laboratory studies, they found that bidders who saw an item displayed against a red background rather than a blue one raised their bids in larger increments. In negotiations, however, where a buyer bargains directly with a seller instead of competing against other buyers, participants shown a red background submitted lower offers than participants shown a blue one. These findings suggest that a red background’s effect on what buyers are willing to pay ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: is greater when items are sold online than when they are sold in person.
depends on whether buyers are competing against other buyers or bargaining with a seller.
disappears once buyers become aware of the color of the background against which the item appears.
depends on how valuable the item being sold is to the buyer.
items.explanation: Red raised bids in auctions, where buyers compete with one another, but lowered offers in negotiations, where a buyer bargains with the seller. Whether red increases or decreases what buyers offer therefore depends on whom they are competing against.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares online and in-person sales; the difference it reports is between auctions and negotiations.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about whether buyers noticed the background color or what happened if they did.

D.why_wrong: The text never varies the value of the items; the outcome flips with the selling format, not with what the item is worth.

sources.what: Bagchi and Cheema 2013, Journal of Consumer Research abstract: data from eBay auctions and the lab show that a red (vs. blue) background elicits higher bid jumps; red backgrounds decrease price offers in negotiations

items.notes: Area: social science (consumer behavior). S7: two settings with opposite outcomes lead to 'depends on' (the 3.14 shape). Distractors: VAR (online vs in person), OUT (awareness), VAR (item value).

fixes: source replaced: the cited ScienceDaily release describes only simulated eBay scenarios, while the passage says “an analysis of eBay auctions”; the paper’s abstract (doi 10.1086/666466) states “data from eBay auctions and the lab”, so the premise stands with that source
review.source_checked: Bagchi and Cheema 2013, JCR abstract via OpenAlex: eBay and lab data show higher bid jumps with red, lower negotiation offers with red

items.subtype: T1 link: a pattern across islands links wariness to predation
items.passage: Animals on islands, where predators are often scarce, have long been described by naturalists as unusually tame. To measure this tendency, biologists William Cooper Jr., Alexander Pyron, and Theodore Garland Jr. compiled data on flight initiation distance, or how close an approaching person can get before an animal flees, for 66 lizard species from mainland and island populations around the world. Island lizards generally allowed people to come considerably closer than mainland lizards did, and the shortest flight initiation distances occurred on islands located farthest from a mainland. These patterns suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: lizards on large islands flee sooner than lizards on small islands do.
lizards on remote islands are less able to detect approaching people than mainland lizards are.
lizards’ readiness to flee may diminish where predators are fewer, as they likely are on islands far from a mainland.
island lizards will gradually become warier as people visit islands more often.
items.explanation: Lizards fled at shorter distances on islands than on the mainland, and shortest of all on the most remote islands, places where predators are likely to be scarcest. The pattern links lizards’ wariness to the number of predators they face.

A.why_wrong: The text compares islands by their distance from a mainland, not by their size.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that island lizards detect people less well; the measure is how close a person gets before they flee.

D.why_wrong: The study compared lizards at one time and makes no prediction about how their behavior will change.

sources.what: island lizards have shorter flight initiation distances than mainland lizards, and the distance decreases as distance from the mainland increases; 66 species (Cooper, Pyron, Garland 2014)

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S8: a repeated pattern (island vs mainland, remote vs near) leads to a link with predation. Distractors: VAR (island size, which the study found no clear effect of), CAUSE (detection), FUT.

review.source_checked: ScienceDaily 2014: Cooper, Pyron, Garland, 66 lizard species, island lizards approachable more closely, more so on remote islands, predator scarcity

items.subtype: T6 function: what carrying an object makes possible
items.passage: Aboriginal peoples of Australia have long used message sticks to communicate between communities. A message stick is a piece of wood carved with markings distinctive to the group that sent it. The markings do not spell out the message, which the messenger delivers by speaking. Along the way, the messenger may travel through the territories of several other groups, presenting the stick to the elders of each. The messenger most likely carries the stick so that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the messenger can read the message from the marks if any of it is forgotten.
the groups along the way can tell who sent the messenger and will allow safe passage.
the elders can keep the stick as payment for letting the messenger rest on their land.
the messenger can use the stick for protection against animals during the journey.
items.explanation: The marks on a message stick show which group sent it, but they do not record the message. Because the messenger shows the stick to the elders of each group along the way, the stick most likely tells them who sent the messenger so they will let the messenger pass.

A.why_wrong: The text says the marks do not spell out the message, so the messenger could not read the message from them.

C.why_wrong: The text says the messenger shows the stick to the elders, not that the elders keep it, and it never mentions payment.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions animals or any use of the stick as a tool or weapon.

sources.what: message sticks helped secure safe passage: the messenger met the elders of each group to show the stick and ask permission to pass; the stick accompanied a verbal message

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (Aboriginal Australian communication). S9 easy: what an object is for. Distractors: REV (read the message), OUT (payment), OUT (protection). Messenger kept gender-neutral.

review.source_checked: Queensland Museum blog: marks distinctive to the sending group, the stick supports the carrier’s oral message, shown to elders of each group as a passport for safe passage

items.subtype: T1 conclusion from a two-condition comparison
items.passage: Researchers at the University of Sussex in England wanted to determine whether horses respond to the emotions displayed on human faces. In their experiment, they showed 28 horses large photographs of people’s faces, some with happy expressions and some with angry ones. When the horses viewed the angry faces, they tended to turn their heads to look at the photographs with their left eye. Many animals use that eye when looking at something threatening. The horses’ heart rates also increased more rapidly when they looked at the angry faces than when they looked at the happy ones. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: horses may be able to tell the difference between angry and happy human faces.
horses usually prefer to look at people with their right eye rather than with their left eye.
horses that live around many people are calmer than horses that live around only a few people.
horses can recognize the faces of people they have met before.
items.explanation: The horses reacted differently to the two kinds of photographs: with angry faces, they used the eye many animals use for threats, and their heart rates rose faster. This suggests that horses can tell angry human faces from happy ones.

B.why_wrong: The text says the horses turned to look at the angry faces with their left eye; it reports no general preference for the right eye.

C.why_wrong: The study did not compare horses that live around different numbers of people.

D.why_wrong: The study used photographs of people’s faces and never tested whether horses recognize people they already know.

sources.what: Smith, Proops, Grounds, Wathan, McComb 2016, Biology Letters (University of Sussex): 28 horses shown photographs of happy and angry human faces; angry faces drew a left-gaze bias and a faster rise in heart rate

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S1 easy: two conditions, one outcome difference, key one step more general. Distractors: REV, VAR, OUT.

fixes: source URL (Sussex news page) returns 404; replaced with the paper’s DOI, whose record confirms 28 horses, left-gaze bias and faster heart-rate rise for angry faces
review.source_checked: Smith et al. 2016, Biology Letters (Semantic Scholar record)

items.subtype: T4 purpose: a behavior that increases once food is stolen
items.passage: Eastern gray squirrels bury numerous nuts each autumn and dig them up later, but other animals frequently find the hidden nuts and steal them. Biologists Michael Steele and Sylvia Halkin, working with colleagues, noticed that a squirrel would sometimes dig a hole and pretend to bury a nut while actually keeping the nut in its mouth. The squirrel would then cover the empty hole and walk away. When the researchers began digging up and removing the nuts that squirrels had really buried, the squirrels made more of these pretend burials. This suggests that the squirrels ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: forget where they have buried nuts after their hiding places have been raided.
prefer to bury nuts in places where other squirrels have already dug.
make empty hiding places to fool animals that might steal their food.
leave some of their nuts behind for the animals that dig up their hiding places.
items.explanation: The squirrels made more pretend burials once their real hiding places began to be raided. Since the empty holes increased in response to theft, they most likely serve to mislead animals that might steal the squirrels’ food.

A.why_wrong: The squirrels kept the nuts in their mouths and covered empty holes on purpose, which is not the same as forgetting where nuts were buried.

B.why_wrong: The text never says where the squirrels chose to dig or whether other squirrels had dug there before.

D.why_wrong: The squirrels kept their nuts in their mouths while pretending to bury them, so they were not leaving nuts for the animals that raid their hiding places.

sources.what: Steele (Wilkes University) described deceptive caching, digging and covering holes without the nut; Halkin and her students (Central Connecticut State University) found that when they acted as thieves and dug up caches, squirrels used more anti-pilfering behaviors, including deceptive caching; both are authors of Steele et al. 2008, Animal Behaviour

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S6 easy: pretend burials rise once real caches are raided, so they target thieves (the 1.10 crow shape). Distractors: CAUSE, OUT, REV.

fixes: passage credited the thief experiment to Steele on a Pennsylvania campus; the cited article credits it to Sylvia Halkin’s team (Central Connecticut State University), Steele’s coauthor on the 2008 paper: now “Biologists Michael Steele and Sylvia Halkin, working with colleagues”, location dropped
“many more” pretend burials softened to “more” (the source says squirrels used more anti-pilfering behaviors) in passage and explanation; re-solved blind, C only
review.source_checked: NWF National Wildlife 2008: Steele described deceptive caching; Halkin and students acted as thieves and squirrels used more anti-pilfering behaviors, including deceptive caching

removed.reason: subject reused: the Durrington Walls feast pigs study (Madgwick et al. 2019) is item 4 of spec/rw/fidelity/round1/sets/text_structure_and_purpose.txt, which WAVE.md bars; the writer also flagged it as the batch's one subject with some fame
